title: Friction on an incline
summary: Tilt your axes along the ramp, split weight into mg sin θ and mg cos θ, and see why the normal force shrinks and mass cancels out of acceleration.

mass.label: $m$
mass.meaning: mass of the block on the incline, in kilograms
mass.body: Scales both the downhill pull ($mg\sin\theta$) and friction ($\mu_k mg\cos\theta$) by the same factor, so it cancels out of the sliding acceleration.
mass.example: A $5\text{ kg}$ block weighs $49\text{ N}$ when $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
mass.analogy: Adding more bricks to a crate increases both its downhill pull and its grip on the ramp in lockstep.

theta.label: $\theta$
theta.meaning: angle of the ramp measured from the horizontal, in degrees
theta.body: Raising $\theta$ increases the downhill pull ($\sin\theta$ rises) and reduces the normal push ($\cos\theta$ falls), doubly helping the block slide.
theta.analogy: Tilting a book steeper until an eraser on the cover breaks loose.

mu_k.label: $\mu_k$
mu_k.meaning: coefficient of kinetic friction between block and ramp (no units)
mu_k.body: Measures how rough the two sliding surfaces are against each other. Larger $\mu_k$ means stronger {kinetic_fric|kinetic friction}.
mu_k.example: With $\mu_k = 0.25$ and $N = 39.2\text{ N}$, kinetic friction is $9.8\text{ N}$.
mu_k.analogy: Swapping polished wood for sandpaper on the ramp surface.

weight.label: $mg$
weight.meaning: gravitational force pulling straight down, in newtons
weight.body: Always vertical — never tilted! To solve incline problems, split it into $mg\sin\theta$ down the slope and $mg\cos\theta$ into the slope.
weight.example: For $m = 5\text{ kg}$ and $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$: $W = mg = 49\text{ N}$.
weight.analogy: A plumb line hanging straight toward the floor regardless of how steep the ramp is.

normal.label: $N$
normal.meaning: normal force pushing perpendicular out of the ramp, in newtons
normal.body: On an incline with no other perpendicular forces, $N = mg\cos\theta$ — always **less** than $mg$ whenever $\theta > 0$.
normal.analogy: A bathroom scale tilted on a ramp reads only the perpendicular squeeze, not your full weight.

friction.label: $f_k$
friction.meaning: kinetic friction opposing the slide (acting up along the ramp), in newtons
friction.body: Given by $f_k = \mu_k N = \mu_k mg\cos\theta$ while sliding. When at rest, {static_fric|static friction} matches $mg\sin\theta$ up to $\mu_s N$.
friction.example: With $\mu_k = 0.25$ and $N = 39.2\text{ N}$, $f_k = 9.8\text{ N}$ up the slope.
friction.analogy: The drag you feel rubbing your palm uphill while sliding down a wooden slide.

accel.label: $a$
accel.meaning: acceleration of the block down the ramp, in m/s²
accel.body: From {newton2|Newton's second law} along the slope: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$ whenever the block slides.
accel.analogy: How fast the block picks up speed as it races down the ramp.

tilted_axes.title: Why tilt the coordinate axes?
tilted_axes.body: Put the $x$-axis **along the ramp** and the $y$-axis **perpendicular** to it. Then [normal:$N$], [friction:$f_k$], and [accel:$a$] all lie cleanly on an axis, leaving only [weight:$mg$] to split into two {vectors|components}.
tilted_axes.useWhen: setting up any {fbd|free-body diagram} on an inclined plane.

slide_threshold.title: When does a block start to slide?
slide_threshold.body: A resting block begins to slide only when the downhill pull exceeds maximum {static_fric|static friction}: $mg\sin\theta > \mu_s mg\cos\theta$. Dividing both sides by $mg\cos\theta$ cancels [mass:mass] and leaves **$\tan\theta > \mu_s$**.
slide_threshold.useWhen: deciding whether a block stays put or starts sliding down a rough ramp.
slide_threshold.example: At $\theta = 30°$, $\tan 30° \approx 0.577$, so a block with $\mu_s = 0.60$ will not budge.

sections.title: Tilt the axes, split one vector
sections.body:
A block on a rough ramp feels three forces in its {fbd|free-body diagram}: {weight_card|weight} straight down, the {normal_card|normal force} perpendicular to the surface, and friction along the surface.

The secret to making the algebra effortless is {tilted_axes|tilting your axes} to match the ramp. Only [weight:$mg$] needs to be resolved into {vectors|components}: $mg\sin\theta$ pulls down the slope, while $mg\cos\theta$ presses into the slope and sets [normal:$N$].

sections.title: Four steps for every incline problem
sections.note: parallel = along the slope; perpendicular = at 90° to the slope

rows.note: at [theta:$\theta = 0°$] (flat ground), $\sin 0° = 0$ and $\cos 0° = 1$ — quick check for which trig function goes where
the block neither sinks into nor flies off the ramp, so $\Sigma F_\perp = 0$

rows.text: Friction: {static_fric|$f_s \le \mu_s N$} at rest; [friction:$f_k = \mu_k N$] while sliding
rows.note: check {slide_threshold|$\tan\theta > \mu_s$} first if the block starts from rest
[mass:mass] cancels completely — heavy and light blocks with the same [mu_k:$\mu_k$] share the same acceleration

sections.title: Worked problem
sections.body:
A [mass:$5\text{ kg}$] crate slides down a rough ramp inclined at [theta:$\theta = 37°$] with [mu_k:$\mu_k = 0.25$].

Taking $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 37° = 0.6$, and $\cos 37° = 0.8$, find the [normal:normal force $N$], the [friction:kinetic friction $f_k$], and the [accel:acceleration $a$] down the ramp.

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: resolve weight first — everything else flows from those two components

routes.title: Route A: tilted axes (perpendicular first, then parallel)
routes.why: Perpendicular {equilibrium|equilibrium} gives [normal:$N$], which unlocks {kinetic_fric|$f_k = \mu_k N$}, and then {newton2|$\Sigma F_\parallel = ma$} yields [accel:$a$].
routes.whyNot: Nothing — this is the cleanest route for every incline problem.

routes.title: Route B: assume $N = mg$ and plug into $f_k = \mu_k mg$
routes.whyNot: On a tilted surface, only the perpendicular piece $mg\cos\theta$ presses into the ramp; using $N = mg$ overestimates friction.

routes.title: Route C: use $mg\cos\theta$ down the slope and $mg\sin\theta$ into it
routes.why: Cosine is often used for horizontal $x$-components.
routes.whyNot: Test $\theta = 0°$: on a flat floor the downhill pull must be **zero**, and $\sin 0° = 0$ whereas $\cos 0° = 1$.

sections.notUsed: Not used: static friction coefficient $\mu_s$. The problem states the crate is already sliding, so kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ acts.

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: hover each step to link the forces on the ramp

steps.move: Compute the total [weight:weight] of the [mass:$5\text{ kg}$] crate.
steps.whyNot: Do not confuse mass ($5\text{ kg}$) with force ($49\text{ N}$).

steps.why: With {tilted_axes|tilted axes}, $a_\perp = 0$, so [normal:$N$] balances the perpendicular piece $mg\cos\theta$ of [weight:weight].
steps.whyNot: Do not set $N = 49\text{ N}$: tilting the ramp takes part of the load along the slope.

steps.move: Calculate [friction:kinetic friction] opposing the slide up the ramp.
steps.why: Because the crate slides down the ramp, {kinetic_fric|kinetic friction} acts **up** the ramp with size $\mu_k N$.
steps.whyNot: Do not multiply $\mu_k$ by total weight $49\text{ N}$ — friction depends on the normal force $N$, not $W$.

steps.move: Find the net force parallel to the ramp (downward component minus friction).
steps.why: Downhill gravity ($29.4\text{ N}$) and uphill [friction:friction] ($9.8\text{ N}$) act in opposite directions along the same line.
steps.whyNot: Do not add them together: friction opposes the downward slide.

steps.move: Divide by [mass:mass] using {newton2|Newton's second law} to get [accel:acceleration].
steps.why: Notice the mass-free check: $a = g(\sin 37° - \mu_k\cos 37°) = 9.8(0.6 - 0.25 \times 0.8) = 9.8(0.4) = 3.92\text{ m/s}^2$.
steps.whyNot: Do not forget to divide by $m = 5\text{ kg}$; $19.6\text{ N}$ is the net force, not the acceleration.

sections.title: Explore the rough ramp
sections.note: drag θ, μ, and m (uses g = 9.8 m/s² and μ_s = μ_k = μ); hover any force arrow to highlight its part, and raise μ past tan θ to make the block stick

sections.title: Check yourself
items: **Normal force**: on a ramp with no extra vertical pushes, [normal:$N = mg\cos\theta$] is always **smaller** than [weight:$mg$].
**Mass cancels**: drag [mass:$m$] on the ramp widget above — every force scales with $m$, yet [accel:$a$] never changes!
**Slide threshold**: a resting block slides only when {slide_threshold|$\tan\theta > \mu_s$}; at $\theta = 30°$ ($\tan 30° \approx 0.577$), set $\mu \ge 0.58$ and watch $a$ drop to $0$.
**Static friction trap**: if the block is **not** sliding, actual {static_fric|static friction} equals $mg\sin\theta$, **not** $\mu_s N$.
**Limiting cases**: at $\theta = 0°$ (flat) $N = mg$ and $a = 0$; at $\theta = 90°$ (vertical wall) $N = 0$, $f_k = 0$, and $a = g$ (free fall).

sections.title: Recall
sections.note: use g = 9.8 m/s² unless stated otherwise

questions.q: A $4\text{ kg}$ block rests on a $60°$ incline ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, $\cos 60° = 0.5$). What is the normal force $N$ from the ramp?
questions.why: $N = mg\cos 60° = 4(9.8)(0.5) = 19.6\text{ N}$. Note that $39.2\text{ N}$ is full weight $mg$, and $33.9\text{ N}$ mistakenly uses $\sin 60°$.

questions.q: A wooden crate is placed at rest on a ramp at $\theta = 37°$ ($\tan 37° = 0.75$) with $\mu_s = 0.80$. What happens when you let go?
options: It slides down because gravity always beats static friction on a steep ramp
It slides only if the crate has a large enough mass
questions.why: By {slide_threshold|the slide condition}, sliding requires $\tan\theta > \mu_s$ regardless of mass. Since $0.75 < 0.80$, static friction holds it.

questions.q: You double the mass of a block sliding down a rough ramp while keeping $\theta$ and $\mu_k$ fixed. What happens to its acceleration $a$?
options: It doubles because the downhill pull $mg\sin\theta$ doubles
It halves because kinetic friction doubles
questions.why: Downhill pull ($mg\sin\theta$), friction ($\mu_k mg\cos\theta$), and inertia ($m$) all double together, so $m$ cancels in $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$.

questions.q: A $2\text{ kg}$ block stays at rest on a $30°$ ramp ($g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 30° = 0.5$) with $\mu_s = 0.70$. What is the static friction force $f_s$ acting on it?
questions.why: Because the block is in {equilibrium|equilibrium}, {static_fric|static friction} matches the downhill pull: $f_s = mg\sin 30° = 2(9.8)(0.5) = 9.8\text{ N}$ (below $f_{s,\max} \approx 11.9\text{ N}$).
